The p53-MDM2 feedback loop and single-cell moment analysis: a simulation and real-data study

Built on the higher-order moment framework of Raharinirina et al. (2021), Patterns 2, 100332.

Contents
1. Overview · 2. The p53-MDM2 loop and Nutlin-3 · 3. Methods · 4. Results (4.1-4.10) · 5. Discussion and conclusions · References

1. Overview

We build a stochastic model of the p53-MDM2 gene circuit, generate synthetic single-cell RNA-seq from it, and ask a focused question: can the p53→MDM2 regulatory interaction be detected—and correctly directed—from mRNA measurements? We answer it first on simulations and then on experimental data, comparing classical dependence measures with the moment-based inference method of Raharinirina et al. (2021).

Summary of findings. The regulatory signal is real and detectable, but it resides in higher-order moments and in dynamics rather than in simple correlation; realistic technical noise (library size) and cell-cycle covariation confound naive correlation; and only moment-based inference or time-resolved/conditioned statistics recover the directed edge p53→MDM2.

2. The p53-MDM2 feedback loop and Nutlin-3

p53 is a tumour-suppressor transcription factor whose abundance is governed by a two-arm loop with the oncoprotein MDM2:

  • Arm 1 (transcriptional, positive): p53 activates transcription of the MDM2 gene, raising MDM2 mRNA and then MDM2 protein.
  • Arm 2 (post-translational, negative): MDM2, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, targets p53 for proteasomal degradation, lowering p53.
p53 turns MDM2 on; MDM2 turns p53 off. Nutlin-3 blocks arm 2.

The two arms constitute a negative feedback loop. Because arm 1 passes through an mRNA intermediate, the loop carries an intrinsic delay, and a delayed negative feedback loop tends to oscillate; deterministically the oscillation is damped, but molecular noise renders it self-sustaining—the p53 pulses observed in single cells (Lahav et al., 2004; Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2006; Proctor & Gray, 2008).

Nutlin-3 and its clinical analogue idasanutlin occupy the p53-binding pocket of MDM2 (Vassilev et al., 2004), abolishing arm 2. p53 accumulates; because arm 1 remains intact, elevated p53 keeps driving MDM2 transcription, yet the additional MDM2 protein cannot restrain p53—the loop is opened. Since the drug acts through p53, it activates p53 targets only in TP53 wild-type cells, which provides a biological negative control on real data (Section 4.7).

Opening the loop removes one arrow, not the whole pathway. Nutlin blocks the reverse inhibitory arm MDM2 protein ⊢ p53, but it does not block p53's transcription-factor activity. The forward branches therefore remain: p53 → MDM2 mRNA and p53 → CDKN1A mRNA. Under Nutlin the observable target-gene structure is consequently the common-driver fork MDM2 mRNA ← p53 protein → CDKN1A mRNA, even though the negative-feedback cycle is open.

3. Methods

3.1 Stochastic model and the Gillespie algorithm

Molecular species are integer counts evolving as a Markov-jump process; each reaction j has a propensity aj(x). The Gillespie stochastic simulation algorithm draws the waiting time to the next event and the identity of that event (Gillespie, 1976):

tau = (1/a0) ln(1/r1), a0 = sum_j aj(x) choose j*: smallest j with sum_{k≤j} ak > r2 a0; x ← x + sj* (r1,r2 ~ U(0,1))

We reuse the exact engine of Raharinirina et al. (2021) (src/ssa.py) and a numba-accelerated, verified-equivalent implementation (src/fast_ssa.py).

3.2 The p53-MDM2 model

Species: p53 mRNA, p53 protein, MDM2 mRNA, MDM2 protein. p53 transcription is constant; MDM2 transcription is activated by p53 (Hill function); p53 degradation by MDM2 is saturable (Michaelis-Menten). Nutlin efficacy scales the degradation rate by (1 - nutlin).

MDM2 transcription (arm 1): ktxn P^n / (Kd^n + P^n) (P = p53) p53 degradation (arm 2): (1 - nutlin) kdeg D P / (Km + P) (D = MDM2)

Unless a result states otherwise, the four-species simulations start from the basal state (TP53 mRNA, p53 protein, MDM2 mRNA, MDM2 protein) = (15, 30, 20, 50). Figure 4 is the explicit exception: to reproduce the start-up visualization in Figure 3 of Raharinirina et al. (2021), all four species begin at zero and the mean-expression path therefore starts at the origin.

Three-gene p53-MDM2-CDKN1A extension used in Figure 13D-E

To test whether conditioning can separate a common-driver correlation from a direct regulatory edge, we extend the four-species loop to six species: TP53 mRNA (mP), p53 protein (P), MDM2 mRNA (mM), MDM2 protein (M), CDKN1A mRNA (mC) and CDKN1A protein (C). The model has 13 reaction channels: transcription, mRNA degradation, translation and protein degradation for each gene, plus MDM2-dependent p53 degradation. MDM2 and CDKN1A transcription are separate Hill functions of the same p53-protein driver:

aMDM2 txn(P) = kM P^nM / (KM^nM + P^nM) + kM0 aCDKN1A txn(P) = kC P^nC / (KC^nC + P^nC) + kC0 aMDM2-dep p53 deg(P,M) = (1 - u) kMP M P / (Km + P)

Here u is Nutlin efficacy. Figure 13D-E uses u = 1, so the last propensity is zero: the MDM2-protein ⊢ p53 arm is fully removed, while both p53-driven transcriptional arms remain.

ProcessParameters used (per min; molecule-count constants where applicable)
TP53transcription 3.0; mRNA decay 0.20; translation 4.0; basal p53-protein decay 0.02
MDM2 ⊢ p53maximum MDM2-dependent p53 degradation 2.0; Michaelis constant Km = 120
p53 → MDM2maximum transcription 6.0; KM = 80; Hill coefficient nM = 4; basal transcription 0.05
MDM2 turnovermRNA decay 0.10; translation 1.2; protein decay 0.30
p53 → CDKN1Amaximum transcription 5.0; KC = 70; Hill coefficient nC = 3; basal transcription 0.05
CDKN1A turnovermRNA decay 0.08; translation 1.0; protein decay 0.15

We simulate 4000 independent cells with the Gillespie direct algorithm, using initial state (mP, P, mM, M, mC, C) = (15, 30, 20, 50, 15, 40) molecules, random seed 93, and 21 retained observation times from 0 to 80 min in 4-min increments. These are exact stochastic reaction counts with intrinsic molecular noise; no dropout, library-size factor, negative-binomial sampling or other technical scRNA-seq noise is added. The full 4000 x 6 x 21 array is cached in data/cache_step9_three_gene_nutlin.npz, allowing Figures 13D-E to be redrawn without rerunning the simulation. The model, accelerated simulator and cache-generation code are saved in src/model_three_gene.py, src/fast_ssa_three_gene.py and analysis/step9b_three_gene_nutlin.py, respectively. The cache also stores the species order, initial state, parameter names and values, Nutlin efficacy, seeds and number of cells.

For Figure 13E, one time is sampled uniformly from the 20 post-Nutlin observations (4-80 min) for each cell (snapshot seed 101). The two conditioning variables summarize the p53-protein input seen by each target before measurement:

Zg(t) = sum_{s≤t} Hg(P(s)) exp[-gammag(t-s)] Delta t, Hg(P) = P^ng / (Kg^ng + P^ng), g in {MDM2, CDKN1A}

The exponential weights account for loss of earlier transcriptional input through target-mRNA decay. Partial correlation is then the Pearson correlation between the residuals after separately regressing MDM2 mRNA and CDKN1A mRNA on the two-column matrix Z. This conditions on the actual protein-level common driver available in the synthetic model.

3.3 Moments

raw moment: E[A^l1 B^l2](t) = (1/N) sum_n a_n^l1 b_n^l2 (A = p53 mRNA, B = MDM2 mRNA) covariance: Cov(A,B) = E[AB] - E[A]E[B] skewness: E[(A-mu)^3] / sigma^3

3.4 Dependence measures

MeasureCapturesSymmetric?
Pearson / Spearmanlinear / monotone correlationyes
Mutual informationany dependence (kNN estimator)yes
HSIC, distance correlationany (nonlinear) dependence; zero iff independentyes

These answer "are A and B related?" but not "which regulates which?" nor "directly or through a third factor?".

3.5 Technical-noise model (Splatter)

library size s ~ LogNormal; counts ~ NB(mean = true * s, dispersion = BCV) dropout probability: pi(mu) = 1 / (1 + exp(-k (ln mu - x0)))
The shared per-cell factor s multiplies every gene and therefore induces spurious gene-gene correlation (Zappia et al., 2017); see Section 4.6.

3.6 Direction and conditioning

Granger (1-step): does A(t) improve prediction of B(t+1) beyond B(t)? Partial correlation of B and C given A (dependence NOT explained by A): residual form: rB = B - fit(B~A), rC = C - fit(C~A); pcorr(B,C|A) = corr(rB, rC) closed form: pcorr(B,C|A) = ( rBC - rBA rCA ) / sqrt( (1 - rBA^2)(1 - rCA^2) ) where rBC, rBA, rCA are ordinary Pearson correlations

Intuition: regress out the common driver A from both variables and correlate what remains; if B and C are associated only because both depend on A, the residuals are uncorrelated (pcorr ≈ 0). Conditional dependence measures are nonlinear analogues (condition on A instead of removing a linear fit). Granger causality is due to Granger (1969); distance correlation to Székely et al. (2007) and HSIC to Gretton et al. (2005). The use of conditioning (partial correlation / conditional independence) to distinguish direct regulation from common-cause correlation follows the causal-inference framework of Pearl (2009), applied to gene networks by de la Fuente et al. (2004) and Schäfer & Strimmer (2005).

3.7 Moment-based inference (Raharinirina et al., 2021)

A library of effective mRNA-level reactions is fitted so that the modelled moment dynamics match the data, closing higher moments with cubic splines and minimizing a non-linear least-squares residual; a 2x2 directed network is then read off:

dm/dt = A(theta) m + B(theta) u(t) (u = higher moments, from data splines) theta_hat = argmin_{theta≥0} sum_d || m(t_d|theta) - m_data(t_d) ||^2

3.8 Permutation z-score

Because Pearson, MI, HSIC and dCor lie on different scales, their raw values are not comparable. To test "is the dependence real?" on a common scale we build a null by shuffling one variable (destroying any relationship), recompute the statistic B times, and standardize:

z = ( s_obs - mean(s_null) ) / std(s_null) p = fraction of permutations with |s_perm - mean| ≥ |s_obs - mean|

Interpretation. z is the number of standard deviations by which the measured dependence exceeds chance. z ≈ 0 means nothing beyond chance; z > 2 corresponds roughly to p < 0.05 (a detection); larger z means stronger evidence. Being unitless, z places all measures on the same footing (Sections 4.6-4.7).

4. Results

Each subsection presents one figure with a formal caption and an interpretation. Sample sizes are stated in every step.

4.1  Stochastic vs deterministic dynamics: intrinsic noise sustains p53 pulses, and Nutlin-3 opens the loop

Deterministic ODE integration plus 4 stochastic (Gillespie) cells per condition; horizon 1500 min, sampled every 2 min. Few single cells are shown on purpose so individual traces remain legible.

In the closed loop the mean-field ODE exhibits a damped oscillation that relaxes to a stable focus, whereas the stochastic simulation of the identical reaction network produces sustained, irregular oscillations. This dichotomy—deterministically damped but stochastically sustained—is the mechanism by which discrete, noisy molecular events continually re-excite the loop, and it reproduces the discrete p53 'pulses' reported in single living cells (Lahav et al., 2004; Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2006). It is the same qualitative behaviour identified in the mechanistic stochastic model of Proctor & Gray (2008).

Full Nutlin-3 inhibition (right) removes the MDM2-mediated degradation of p53 (arm 2). p53 no longer has a fast decay channel and rises to a high plateau in every cell, while the oscillation disappears: the negative feedback is broken and the system is driven to an open-loop steady state. This is the single-cell signature of pharmacological MDM2 inhibition (Vassilev et al., 2004).

4.2  Dose-dependent p53 accumulation, MDM2-mRNA induction, and suppression of oscillation

1500 cells per dose, six Nutlin-3 efficacies; horizon 1600 min; statistics in the late window t ≥ 600 min. Here 'efficacy' is a mechanistic parameter (fraction of p53-MDM2 binding blocked, 0-1), not a drug concentration; the experimental data (Section 4.7) used a single near-saturating dose of 2.5 uM (no dose series was available).

Increasing inhibition raises mean p53 monotonically and steeply near full block (left), consistent with progressive loss of the degradation channel. MDM2 mRNA also rises (centre) but saturates, because transcriptional activation of MDM2 by p53 (arm 1) is bounded by promoter saturation—p53 keeps driving transcription even though the resulting MDM2 protein can no longer act on p53.

The oscillation index (right) is essentially flat at low-to-moderate doses and then collapses near complete inhibition, marking the transition from a functioning (pulsatile) loop to an open loop. Together the three curves quantify the qualitative picture of Fig. 1: arm 1 intact, arm 2 cut.

4.3  Regulatory information resides in the higher-order moments of mRNA counts

3000 cells per condition; snapshots every 15 min up to 1500 min. Only mRNA counts are used, mimicking scRNA-seq.

The mean of p53 mRNA is essentially identical in the two conditions (the two lines overlap near 15 counts), because Nutlin acts on p53 protein stability, not on p53 transcription. An analysis restricted to the mean of this transcript would therefore detect no effect.

The regulatory change is instead written into the higher-order moments: the covariance of the two mRNAs drops from about +10 (closed loop) to approximately 0 (Nutlin), and the skewness of MDM2 mRNA falls markedly. This is a direct, quantitative illustration of the central thesis of Raharinirina et al. (2021): the signature of regulation is distributed across mean, covariance and skewness rather than being captured by the mean alone.

4.4  Joint distribution and moment dynamics of the (p53, MDM2) mRNA pair

4000 cells per condition, with all four dynamic species initialized at zero; 301 raw snapshots every 4 min from 0 to 1200 min. Panels A-B show the t = 300 min population. The raw moment series are stored in data/cache_step4_zero_initial.npz.

In the closed loop the joint cloud is tilted along a positive diagonal (covariance +10.8, correlation +0.43): cells rich in p53 mRNA also tend to be rich in MDM2 mRNA, the fingerprint of an intact transcriptional coupling. Under Nutlin the cloud becomes round and shifts upward (covariance -0.4, correlation -0.01, both effectively zero), with MDM2 mRNA elevated—dependence is lost even though the marginal level of MDM2 mRNA is higher.

Why did the previous version not begin at zero? It inherited the model's basal starting state (15 TP53 mRNAs, 30 p53 proteins, 20 MDM2 mRNAs and 50 MDM2 proteins). Moreover, 15 is exactly the mean steady-state TP53-mRNA count implied by constitutive transcription and decay: dE[mP]/dt = 3.0 - 0.20E[mP], which equals zero at E[mP] = 15. The old green marker therefore correctly appeared at (15,20), and TP53 mRNA had no initial mean change, but that did not reproduce the visual experiment in Patterns2021. The revised Figure 4 instead starts (TP53 mRNA, p53 protein, MDM2 mRNA, MDM2 protein) = (0,0,0,0). Its expected TP53-mRNA start-up is E[mP](t) = 15(1 - exp[-0.20t]), so it rises immediately from zero toward 15 counts. This zero start is a deliberate start-up experiment for Figure 4, not a claim that a treated biological cell contains no p53 or MDM2 at baseline.

Panel C shows that after the start-up transient the two solid p53-mRNA curves coincide, underscoring that the discriminating information lies in the second- and third-order statistics (D-F), not in the first-order mean of p53 mRNA.

4.5  Detecting statistical dependence under dropout with five association measures

4000 cells per condition; snapshot at t = 600 min; five capture efficiencies × six independent noise draws each. HSIC and dCor use a reproducible 1200-cell subsample per draw. The clean snapshot and all summary values are saved in data/cache_step5.npz.

All five measures separate the closed loop from Nutlin when capture is high and lose signal as dropout increases. At full capture, Pearson = 0.431, Spearman = 0.433 and dCor = 0.414 in the closed loop, compared with 0.019, 0.016 and 0.045 under Nutlin. Their similar closed-loop values indicate that the detectable dependence is predominantly monotone and close to linear; dCor does not reveal a large additional nonlinear component here.

The full-capture MI and normalized HSIC values are 0.103 and 0.094 in the closed loop. These smaller numbers do not by themselves mean weaker biological dependence: MI is measured in nats and normalized HSIC has a different scale, so their raw magnitudes cannot be compared with a correlation coefficient. What matters in this figure is their separation from the corresponding Nutlin/no-dependence curve and how rapidly that separation disappears with dropout. Formal cross-method comparison uses permutation z-scores in Figure 7, where the kNN MI estimator indeed shows lower detection power.

This step uses a deliberately idealized noise model (each mRNA molecule retained independently with probability β). The following step replaces it with a published, more realistic model and reveals a confounder that this simple model does not expose.

4.6  Realistic technical noise (Splatter) and the library-size confound

3000 cells per condition; snapshot at t = 600 min; five dropout midpoints × five noise draws; kernel measures subsampled to 1000 cells.

Unlike the idealized model of Fig. 5, the Splatter model applies a shared per-cell library-size factor that multiplies every gene. This induces a spurious positive association between transcripts that are in fact independent, so the Nutlin-3 curves no longer sit at zero for the correlation-type measures. This is a well-known scRNA-seq confounder and a concrete example of the pre-processing pitfalls emphasized by Raharinirina et al. (2021).

The permutation test in Fig. 7 quantifies which apparent detections are real and which are artefacts of library size.

In the closed loop the true dependence is strongly significant for Pearson (z ≈ 6), Spearman (≈ 5.5), HSIC (≈ 12) and distance correlation (≈ 12); mutual information is the exception (z ≈ 0.7), because the kNN MI estimator is a weak, high-variance detector on discrete count data (Section 4.5).

Under Nutlin-3 the two transcripts are genuinely independent, so every bar there should be zero. Instead Pearson (z ≈ 3.5), Spearman (≈ 2.9), HSIC (≈ 3.6) and dCor (≈ 5.3) are all significant false positives, produced by the shared per-cell library-size factor; only mutual information stays near zero (z ≈ 0.7). The correct reading is therefore not that any one statistic is intrinsically 'robust' — the powerful measures all detect the library-size artefact, and MI only escapes because of its low power. The real remedy is explicit library-size normalization, which we apply to the experimental data in Section 4.7.

4.7  Validation on experimental scRNA-seq: MIX-seq DMSO versus idasanutlin

Why not the direct (p53, MDM2) pair, and why does the sign look reversed versus the simulation?

WT line LNCaP, 6 h (n=152 treated). dCor of TP53-MDM2 vs MDM2-CDKN1A.

Our ideal observable is the loop pair (p53, MDM2), and the simulation uses exactly that. On real scRNA-seq, however, TP53 mRNA is a poor readout of p53 activity: p53 is controlled post-translationally, so its transcript barely moves and does not track the protein that actually drives MDM2 transcription. Panel (A) confirms this directly—TP53 mRNA barely changes with the drug (it even dips slightly), while MDM2 and CDKN1A are strongly induced. Panels (B)-(C) show the direct TP53-MDM2 scatter has little structure (dCor 0.07 in DMSO, 0.10 under idasanutlin) and stays weak in both conditions, whereas the p53-target pair MDM2-CDKN1A jumps from 0.12 to 0.38. On mRNA-only data the loop's regulatory coherence is therefore best read from p53-target co-expression, not from the nominal (p53, MDM2) pair—an intrinsic limitation of measuring a post-translationally regulated hub at the mRNA level. We use MDM2-CDKN1A for the rest of this section.

The direction of the drug effect on that pair also differs from the simulation, for a principled reason: cell-to-cell covariance requires both an active regulatory link and heterogeneity in the upstream driver. In the simulation the baseline (no drug) is an actively cycling loop, so covariance is high at baseline and Nutlin—by clamping p53—removes it. In the experiment the baseline (DMSO) is quiescent (low, uniform p53 activity), so target co-expression is low, and it is the drug that switches p53 on heterogeneously, creating the co-expression. Same principle, opposite baseline.

Experimental data from MIX-seq (McFarland et al., 2020): 1886 (DMSO) and 2634 (idasanutlin) QC-passing singlets across a pool of 24 cell lines; the TP53 wild-type line LNCaP contributes n ≈ 100 / 152 cells; permutation tests use B = 200-300.

Idasanutlin sharply induces canonical p53 targets (MDM2, CDKN1A, FDXR, ...) in the TP53-wild-type line LNCaP but not in the TP53-mutant line, as expected for a p53-dependent drug (McFarland et al., 2020). Concomitantly, MDM2 and CDKN1A—two direct p53 targets—become co-expressed under treatment: dCor rises from 0.12 (not significant) to 0.38 (permutation z ≈ 9). The 2x2 control (E) isolates the p53-dependent effect: only the wild-type + idasanutlin condition shows strong co-regulation, while the drug-treated mutant line does not.

A caveat is made explicit in panel F: among all gene pairs, only MDM2-CDKN1A gains dependence upon treatment, whereas housekeeping pairs actually lose covariation—idasanutlin arrests the cell cycle in wild-type cells, removing a global source of gene-gene covariance. Housekeeping pairs are therefore not a perfect negative control in single-cell data; the cleanest control is the isogenic comparison against a non-responding (mutant) line.

Does the effect generalize across cell lines?

All 22 MIX-seq cell lines with ≥ 40 QC-passing cells in both DMSO and idasanutlin (6 h). For each line: p53 response = mean induction of MDM2 + CDKN1A (idasanutlin minus DMSO, log-norm); dCor gain = distance correlation of (MDM2, CDKN1A) in idasanutlin minus in DMSO. Marker area is linearly proportional to the total number of QC-passing cells for that line across both conditions.

There is a positive association (r = +0.44): lines whose p53 targets are induced more strongly by idasanutlin also tend to gain more MDM2-CDKN1A co-expression, consistent with the mechanism above. LNCaP, the wild-type line used throughout this section, sits at the extreme of both axes and is the cleanest example in the panel; CCFSTTG1, NCIH226 and DKMG (moderate p53 response) also show a modest positive gain.

The relationship is noisy, however, and we report it as such rather than overstating it. Two lines with almost no p53 response (RCM1, BT549) show large negative dCor changes, most likely small-sample or line-specific noise rather than a p53-related effect, and they visibly pull down the correlation. With only 22 lines and per-line cell counts of a few hundred, this trend should be read as supportive but not as strong independent confirmation; it motivates, rather than replaces, the single-line analysis with its 2x2 biological control.

Timepoint dependence: 6 h versus 24 h of idasanutlin

Idasanutlin was applied at a single saturating concentration (2.5 uM) and assayed at 6 h and 24 h (MIX-seq has no idasanutlin dose series). WT line LNCaP: 152 vs 102 treated cells.

The two readouts move in opposite directions with time. The mean induction of p53 targets is generally larger at 24 h (summed log-fold induction 6.6 at 6 h vs 9.4 at 24 h), reflecting continued accumulation of target mRNA. In contrast, the cell-to-cell co-expression of MDM2 and CDKN1A is stronger at 6 h (dCor 0.38) than at 24 h (0.26).

This is expected: at 6 h the response is still in its heterogeneous transient, so p53 activity—and hence its targets—varies markedly from cell to cell, maximizing the covariation our measures detect; by 24 h the response has largely saturated and homogenized (and fewer cells are recovered, consistent with arrest/apoptosis), so the mean is higher but the covariation is lower. The rest of this section uses the 6 h timepoint, which gives the cleaner co-regulation signal. Note that 'efficacy' in our simulation (Section 4.2) is a mechanistic fraction-of-binding-blocked in [0,1], whereas 2.5 uM is a single, near-saturating concentration; the two are related monotonically but are not the same quantity.

4.8  Recovering directed regulation from moments: non-linear moment-based inference (Raharinirina et al., 2021)

8000 cells per condition; raw moments up to order 3-4; approximately 49 snapshots used for the fit after discarding the transient and subsampling. Note on noise: the input is clean SSA counts—they carry the intrinsic (molecular) noise that MBI actually exploits, but no technical scRNA-seq noise (dropout, library size) is applied here. This is a best-case test, as in Raharinirina et al. (2021).

Unlike the symmetric dependence measures of the previous steps, MBI returns a directed network. In the closed loop it cleanly recovers the transcriptional edge p53 → MDM2 (A→B = +3.9) and essentially no MDM2 → p53 edge (B→A = 0). The absence of an MDM2 → p53 edge is expected, because the negative arm operates post-translationally on p53 protein and is invisible at the mRNA level. This demonstrates, on our system, the ability of MBI to infer regulatory direction from mRNA moments alone (Raharinirina et al., 2021).

Under Nutlin-3 MBI still recovers a positive p53 → MDM2 edge (A→B = +2.0). This is biologically correct: Nutlin blocks the MDM2–p53 protein interaction, not the transcriptional arm, so p53 continues to drive MDM2 transcription (indeed MDM2 mRNA is elevated). However, the inference is now less clean—it also reports a spurious MDM2 → p53 edge (B→A = -1.1). The reason is identifiability: with the loop open, p53 is clamped at a high, near-constant level and MDM2 mRNA sits on a flat plateau, so the moment time-courses carry little dynamic information for the fit to exploit. MBI is therefore most reliable in the informative, oscillating closed-loop regime; a near-static system yields weaker, noisier network estimates.

Finally, a scope note: MBI works on the moment time-courses and implicitly assumes the observed moments equal the true moments. It de-noises only by averaging over many cells (and by spline-smoothing the higher moments), which suppresses sampling noise—but it does not model technical scRNA-seq artefacts. Because dropout and library-size shifts distort exactly the higher-order moments MBI relies on (Section 4.6), such technical noise would bias the inference; the clean, intrinsic-noise-only setting here is deliberately a best case.

4.9  Endowing dependence measures with direction and conditional specificity

4000 cells per condition for the directional analysis (fluctuation window t ≥ 200 min). Panels D-E use a separate 4000-cell, six-species p53-MDM2-CDKN1A Gillespie simulation. Each independent cell starts from (TP53 mRNA, p53 protein, MDM2 mRNA, MDM2 protein, CDKN1A mRNA, CDKN1A protein) = (15, 30, 20, 50, 15, 40) molecules and is recorded at 21 snapshots, every 4 min from 0 to 80 min, with Nutlin efficacy = 1. This simulation contains intrinsic reaction noise but no dropout, library-size variation or other technical scRNA-seq noise. The random seed is 93; the asynchronous-snapshot seed is 101. The complete output is saved in data/cache_step9_three_gene_nutlin.npz; all 20 kinetic parameters are tabulated in Method 3.2. Real-data partial correlation uses LNCaP (n ≈ 152).

Two ingredients convert the symmetric measures of Sections 4.5-4.6 into causal ones. Direction requires time: using per-cell trajectories, the lagged cross-correlation and lagged distance correlation peak at positive lag for p53→MDM2 (A leads B). In panel C, one-step Granger causality is also strongly asymmetric in the dynamic closed loop (p53→MDM2 = 0.207 versus MDM2→p53 = 0.000), recovering the same direction. Both Granger values are approximately zero under Nutlin because the open-loop mRNA trajectories rapidly settle onto a nearly static plateau, leaving little predictive fluctuation. (Because the lagged measures are symmetric, CB→A(τ)=CA→B(−τ), it is enough to show positive lags only: over τ ≥ 0 the two directional curves are genuinely distinct, and the p53→MDM2 curve exceeding MDM2→p53 there means p53 fluctuations precede MDM2—the temporal-precedence signature of p53→MDM2. The ~4-min peak reflects the transcription/translation delay.) A further advantage of the signed cross-correlation (panel A) is the negative lobe near τ ≈ 16 min: after p53 drives MDM2 up, the negative-feedback arm pulls the system back, giving an anti-correlation (overshoot) at roughly half the loop's oscillation timescale. This lobe is consistent with the closed negative-feedback loop—it is absent under Nutlin (open loop; grey dashed curve) and, being a change of sign, cannot appear in the non-negative distance correlation of panel B.

Panels D and E use an explicit p53-MDM2-CDKN1A simulation. It contains mRNA and protein for all three genes and 13 reaction channels, simulated exactly with the Gillespie direct method. All 4000 cells use the same initial molecular counts and kinetic constants but have independent reaction-event histories, so their variation is intrinsic stochastic variation. Here open loop means that Nutlin removes only the reverse inhibitory arm, MDM2 protein ⊢ p53; it does not inhibit p53 as a transcription factor. At efficacy 1, the effective MDM2-dependent p53 degradation constant is exactly zero, while the forward branches p53 → MDM2 mRNA and p53 → CDKN1A mRNA remain. This gives the common-driver fork MDM2 mRNA ← p53 protein → CDKN1A mRNA. Panel D plots log2[(mean count at t + 1)/(mean count at t = 0 + 1)]. TP53 mRNA remains close to baseline because its transcription is constitutive in the model, whereas p53 protein rises continuously to more than 6 log2-fold above baseline after MDM2-mediated degradation is blocked. MDM2 and CDKN1A mRNAs also increase and then plateau because both forward transcriptional branches remain active. This separation between a nearly unchanged TP53 transcript and strongly accumulating p53 protein illustrates why TP53 mRNA is a poor proxy for p53 activity in scRNA-seq. The rising MDM2 transcript cannot restore feedback because Nutlin prevents its protein product from degrading p53. CDKN1A is a canonical p53 target associated with cell-cycle arrest; this minimal model simulates its expression but does not simulate the cell cycle itself.

Panel E converts the trajectories into a synthetic asynchronous scRNA-seq-like snapshot without adding technical noise: each of the 4000 cells contributes exactly one observation, sampled uniformly from the 20 post-treatment times (4-80 min). The resulting response-phase heterogeneity makes MDM2 and CDKN1A strongly correlated (r = 0.602). The conditioning covariates are two target-specific, exponentially weighted histories of p53-protein Hill activity, using each target's Hill constant, Hill coefficient and mRNA-decay rate. They represent the shared p53 input accumulated before the sampled time. Regressing both target mRNAs on these covariates and correlating the residuals reduces the partial correlation to -0.001. Thus the tall marginal bar reflects the common p53 fork, rather than a direct MDM2-CDKN1A edge. On the real data (panel F), conditioning MDM2-CDKN1A on an mRNA p53-activity proxy lowers their correlation only slightly (0.43 to 0.38), so it does not establish a direct edge; the proxy does not measure protein-level p53 activity without error (Kuroki & Pearl, 2014). Partial correlation is nonetheless a standard tool for pruning indirect edges in gene networks (de la Fuente et al., 2004; Schäfer & Strimmer, 2005).

A fundamental limitation applies: these directional estimators require per-cell time series, whereas scRNA-seq destroys each cell at measurement and yields only population snapshots. Direction on real data must therefore come from population moment dynamics (MBI, Section 4.8) or from RNA velocity, rather than from lagged single-cell statistics.

4.10  Robustness and reproducibility

Because the simulator is stochastic, we separate two notions. Reproducibility: the numba-parallel Gillespie engine is seeded per cell, so a given seed reproduces the ensemble bit-for-bit (verified: same seed → identical arrays; a RECOMPUTE flag forces a fresh run). Robustness: whether the conclusions—not the exact numbers—survive changing the seed. Averages over thousands of cells (Sections 4.1-4.4) are inherently stable; the single-realization estimates (the permutation z-scores of Section 4.6 and the MBI network of Section 4.8) are the ones that need checking. For the permutation test we already average over five noise draws; for MBI we re-ran the inference over several seeds:

ConditionA→B (p53→MDM2)B→A (MDM2→p53)
CLOSED loop+1.36 ± 0.60  (0.8, 1.0, 2.2)  always positive0.00 ± 0.00  always zero
NUTLIN-3+1.03 ± 0.40  (1.4, 0.5, 1.2)  always positive−0.26 ± 0.18  (−0.4, 0, −0.3)  unstable

(3 seeds, N = 2500 cells; the main Section 4.8 figure uses N = 8000.) The direction p53→MDM2 is robust: A→B is positive in every seed and in both conditions (including Nutlin, where the transcriptional arm remains intact), while a stable reverse edge never appears (B→A is exactly zero in the closed loop and only a small, sign-unstable value under Nutlin—confirming that the reverse edge seen in a single Nutlin run is an identifiability artefact, not a real edge). The magnitude of the edge, by contrast, varies from seed to seed (A→B ranges 0.5-2.2). The practical lesson: report the inferred direction, which is trustworthy, rather than the precise edge weight, which is not.

5. Discussion and conclusions

  1. Intrinsic noise converts the deterministically-damped p53-MDM2 loop into sustained p53 pulses; Nutlin-3 opens the loop, so p53 accumulates and oscillations cease (Sections 4.1-4.2).
  2. The regulatory signal resides in higher-order moments (covariance, skewness), not in the mean of the p53 transcript (Sections 4.3-4.4), as argued by Raharinirina et al. (2021).
  3. Realistic technical noise (library size) and cell-cycle covariation create spurious correlations that powerful dependence measures (Pearson, Spearman, HSIC, distance correlation) all flag as false positives; only the low-power kNN mutual-information estimator stays near zero. The proper remedy is library-size normalization, not the choice of statistic (Sections 4.6-4.7).
  4. On experimental MIX-seq data the p53 program (MDM2-CDKN1A co-regulation) is detected only in TP53 wild-type cells under idasanutlin, with a clean isogenic mutant control (Section 4.7).
  5. Symmetric measures report association only; the moment-based inference of Raharinirina et al. (2021), and time-resolved/conditioned statistics, recover the directed edge p53→MDM2 and distinguish regulation from mere correlation (Sections 4.8-4.9).
  6. Obtaining direction from single cells ultimately requires dynamics (moments) or RNA velocity, because snapshot scRNA-seq has no per-cell time axis.
